entry.evidence: This observed parasequence stacking pattern is opposite from the traditional sequence stratigraphic models following a maximum marine transgression.

steps.action: Poses the conundrum: the Spirit River clastic wedge shows strongly progradational to aggradational stacking above a maximum transgression, which is the opposite of model expectation and was never discussed before.
steps.quote: Previous studies of the Spirit River Formation never discussed that this third-order clastic wedge has the opposite of the expected parasequence stacking pattern

steps.action: Assembles over 4,000 public well-log suites and logs 29 drill cores for sedimentary structures, trace fossils, lithology, grain size and bioturbation index.
steps.quote: Over 4,000 well penetrations with associated downhole geophysical well log suites were used for correlations within the study area.

steps.action: Calibrates core-defined facies associations and stratigraphic surfaces to gamma-ray, resistivity and density log responses and sets pick criteria for major flooding surfaces and sequence boundaries in uncored wells.
steps.quote: Sequence stratigraphic surfaces and facies associations were calibrated to well log suite responses to correlate numerous wells where core data is unavailable.

steps.action: Checks the log pick of the major flooding surface against the core-observed transgressive surface of marine erosion and finds a 0.3 to 2 m offset, small against parasequence sets of about 15 m.
steps.quote: Thus, the error is minor considering the more than commonly 15 m thick parasequence sets throughout this study area.

steps.action: States the rival readings of thick channel sandstone bodies (incised-valley complexes versus distributary channels), to be separated by stratigraphic character, mapping and scale.
steps.quote: Stratigraphic characteristics, mapping, and scale of channel bodies were used to differentiate between incised-valley complexes and distributary channels

steps.action: Designs a moving stratigraphic datum of local coal seams and flooding surfaces, adjusted datum to datum along the 290 km dip cross-section; rejects the Bluesky top and a single coal seam as datums.
steps.quote: Each datum was adjusted accordingly to the adjacent datum along the length of the cross-section, adding robustness to the stratigraphic architecture

steps.action: Interprets facies associations 1 to 3 from sedimentary structures and ichnology: offshore transition, wave-dominated fluvial-influenced shoreline, and incised-valley fill.
steps.quote: Facies association 1 is interpreted to have been deposited above storm wave base and below fair-weather wave base in an offshore transition depositional environment

steps.action: Excludes distributary channels for FA 3 on four grounds: truncation of regional coals and flooding surfaces, a basinward facies shift, and continuous mappable extent across parasequence sets. A cut-and-fill reading is noted as possible.
steps.quote: Facies association 3 is distinguished from distributary channels by truncating regional coal seams and underlying regional marine flooding surfaces, a basinward shift in facies

steps.action: Interprets facies association 4 as non-marine coastal plain and fluvial channel deposits.
steps.quote: Facies association 4 is interpreted as a non-marine coastal plain and fluvial channels of the Upper Mannville undifferentiated.

steps.action: From a grid of strike and dip cross-sections and gross-sandstone maps, establishes that each younger parasequence-set sandstone is fully offset seaward, giving strongly progradational stacking with little aggradation.
steps.quote: The stacking geometries of parasequence sets indicate a strongly progradational shoreline succession with little aggradation.

steps.action: Compares this geometry with the strongly aggradational stacking of the younger legacy Falher sets described by Leckie (1986).
steps.quote: The geometry of strongly progradational parasequence set sandstone bodies differs significantly from the strongly aggradational parasequence set stacking geometry of the younger Falher parasequence sets.

steps.action: Checks the cross-section A facies architecture against the outcrop-based trends of Zonneveld and Moslow (2004) and finds similar trends.
steps.quote: shows similar trends as described by Zonneveld and Moslow (2004)

steps.action: Identifies ten fourth-order parasequence sets and assigns systems tracts: normal-regressive sets as highstand, and Falher N as a possible lowstand after forced regression that initiated the incised valleys.
steps.quote: The studied interval of the Spirit River Formation consists of ten laterally accreting northward fourth-order parasequence sets

steps.action: Integrates the new framework with the legacy Falher framework on regional cross-section B and divides the formation at a third-order type 2 sequence boundary into Lower (Falher R-I) and Upper (Falher H-A) sequences.
steps.quote: Cross-section B shows the distinct change in Falher parasequence set stacking patterns from strongly progradational to strongly aggradational around townships 62 to 64

steps.action: Adopts the sediment-supply versus accommodation framework of Van Wagoner et al. (1988): S > A gives progradation and A = S gives aggradation.
steps.quote: Fundamentally, stacking patterns represent the interplay of the rates of sediment supply (S) and the creation of accommodation space (A).

steps.action: Infers a consistently high sediment supply from cited drainage scale, extensive coals, greenhouse climate and fluvial incised-valley fills.
steps.quote: A relatively consistent and high rate of sediment supply to the foreland basin is assumed throughout Spirit River Formation deposition

steps.action: Sets cited eustatic curves (an overall Early Albian rise) and tectonic-loading records against the stacking change, and argues that flexural subsidence overprints eustasy.
steps.quote: However, induced flexural subsidence plays a vital role in overprinting the effects of eustatic sea-level within the active Alberta Foreland Basin

steps.action: States the rival control: local subsidence of the Peace River Arch created the accommodation for the aggradational stacking (Leckie 1986; Cant 1996).
steps.quote: The epeirogenic movement of the actively subsiding Peace River Arch during the Early Cretaceous could have formed additional accommodation

steps.action: Rejects Peace River Arch subsidence as the primary control because the non-marine Upper Mannville isopach does not change across the arch boundary.
steps.quote: Therefore, it is interpreted local Peace River Arch subsidence was not primarily controlling increases in the production of available accommodation.

steps.action: Keeps the claim: increased tectonic activity and subsidence raised accommodation to match the high sediment supply, producing aggradation in the Upper Spirit River Formation.
steps.quote: [...] in tectonic activity and associated subsidence resulted in a significant increase in the rate of creation of accommodation space

steps.action: Extends the lesson to clastic wedges in active foreland basins worldwide: they are best treated with observational, locally controlled sequence stratigraphic models.
steps.quote: sedimentary clastic wedges deposited within an active foreland basin worldwide are best suited to an observational data-based sequence stratigraphic model

tree.answer: Yes: strongly progradational parasequence-set stacking above a maximum flooding surface, opposite to model expectation
No; stacking geometry is reconstructed from well-log correlation calibrated to cores
Build the framework, then explain the controls (sediment supply versus accommodation) on stacking patterns
Yes: sediment supply, eustasy, regional tectonic subsidence, Peace River Arch subsidence; also incised valley versus distributary channel
Partly: Peace River Arch control predicts isopach change across the arch boundary
Found, not set: past basin record known from traces
Partly: core check of log picks and agreement with outcrop trends; no sensitivity test of the control interpretation
Tectonic subsidence plus high supply kept as best explanation; Peace River Arch control rejected

end.claim: High sediment influx relative to accommodation produced the strongly progradational Lower Spirit River Formation; sustained supply with increased tectonic subsidence produced the strongly aggradational Upper Spirit River Formation.

decisive_move.sentence: Correlating thousands of core-calibrated well logs across a moving-datum cross-section grid established the strongly progradational stacking of ten Falher parasequence sets, the phenomenon the whole controls argument explains.

gates.evidence: Data were existing public well logs and cores, assembled to build a framework rather than to test a stated hypothesis (p. 2, p. 13). Only the Peace River Arch rival faced a test it could fail (isopach across the arch boundary, p. 14). The tectonic-subsidence claim rests on cited corroboration, with timing 'not concrete' (p. 14). Nothing is reported as fixed before the data were seen.

geoSCOUT software and well database donated by Geologic Systems Ltd.

novelty_claims.quote: Previous studies of the Spirit River Formation never discussed that this third-order clastic wedge has the opposite of the expected parasequence stacking pattern
focusing on fourth-ordered parasequence set scale detail, which few basins in the world can replicate

limits: The XML text holds only the abstract and captions, so most locations are PDF/journal pages. No review file was supplied; the acknowledgments thank an anonymous reviewer, but no review-driven changes can be coded. Sediment supply is assumed from cited drainage, climate and coal evidence, not measured. Accommodation and subsidence are not quantified beyond 10-20 m between Upper sets. The authors state that biostratigraphic age control is poor and that tectonic timing is 'not concrete' (p. 3, p. 14). Individual parasequences were not mapped (p. 3). Cross-sections A and B were selected as 'most representative' from a grid, and the others are not shown (p. 10). Sub-claims and their statuses: facies-association environments are best_explanation; the incised-valley reading is best_explanation, with a cut-and-fill alternative left open (p. 10); the Falher N lowstand designation is tentative ('could be designated', p. 11-12); the division into two third-order sequences is best_explanation ('suggests', p. 14); the worldwide recommendation (p. 15) is untested generalization. Inference: the eustasy rival is dismissed by argument from cited work, not by a test in these data.

disagreements.target: traditional sequence stratigraphic models following a maximum marine transgression
disagreements.support: Regional log and core correlation shows strongly progradational, then aggradational, stacking above the maximum flooding surface; the authors attribute this to local supply and tectonic accommodation in an active foreland basin.
disagreements.quote: This observed parasequence stacking pattern is opposite from the traditional sequence stratigraphic models following a maximum marine transgression.

disagreements.support: Core facies show the parasequence sets are predominantly sandstone, so the authors reassign them Falher Member names.
disagreements.quote: This nomenclature would suggest the ‘Wilrich’ play is a dominantly shaley succession.

disagreements.target: Peace River Arch subsidence as control on aggradational Falher stacking (Leckie, 1986; Cant, 1996)
disagreements.support: The non-marine Upper Mannville isopach does not change significantly across the Peace River Arch boundary on cross-section B.
disagreements.quote: Therefore, it is interpreted local Peace River Arch subsidence was not primarily controlling increases in the production of available accommodation.

alternatives_considered.reason: Bluesky top has depositional relief and erosion; coal seams split, and the architecture is slightly aggradational

alternatives_considered.chosen: Major flooding surface picked at the base of the thick mudstone on logs
alternatives_considered.alternatives: Picking the transgressive surface of marine erosion
alternatives_considered.reason: Transgressive deposits cannot be distinguished from regressive ones without core; chosen for consistency

alternatives_considered.reason: More extensive mapping and correlation objectives
